name: Ginger
aka: Sheng Jiang, Gan Jiang, Zingiber officinale
summary: Cochrane reviews confirm ginger works for pregnancy, chemotherapy and postoperative nausea at about 1-1.5 g daily. Gingerols inhibit COX-2 and 5-LOX, modestly easing osteoarthritis pain, and a 2018 meta-analysis showed lower fasting glucose and HbA1c.
how: Fresh tea: 1-2 inches sliced root steeped 10-15 minutes, 2-3 cups daily. Dried powder 250 mg-1 g capsules 2-4 times daily; for nausea 250 mg every 6 hours or chew crystallized ginger. Use liberally in cooking.
safety: May increase bleeding risk: use cautiously with warfarin, aspirin and clopidogrel and stop 1-2 weeks before surgery. Over 5 g/day causes heartburn, diarrhea and mouth irritation, and it may lower blood sugar with diabetes drugs. Generally safe in pregnancy under 1 g/day; check with your OB/GYN.
origin: A foundational TCM herb: fresh ginger warms the Lungs, dried ginger warms the Spleen and Stomach.

name: Ginseng
aka: Ren Shen, Xi Yang Shen, Panax ginseng
summary: A 2020 meta-analysis of 10 RCTs found improved cognition, especially reaction time and working memory, and a 16-RCT review found significantly lower fasting glucose. Red Korean ginseng shows moderate benefit for erectile dysfunction and it reduces cancer-related fatigue.
how: Standardized extract 200-400 mg daily (4-7% ginsenosides). Decoction: simmer 3-6 root slices 30-60 minutes, once or twice daily. Tincture 1-2 mL two to three times daily. TCM cycles it 2-3 weeks on, 1-2 weeks off.
safety: Can cause insomnia, headache, digestive upset and agitation, especially Asian ginseng. May interact with warfarin, diabetes medications (hypoglycemia), MAOIs and stimulants. Avoid in uncontrolled hypertension and estrogen-sensitive conditions, and during acute febrile infection.
origin: The 'King of Herbs', tonifying Qi and calming the spirit; American ginseng suits heat signs.

name: Astragalus
summary: Polysaccharides and astragalosides stimulate macrophages, NK cells and T-lymphocytes. A 2019 meta-analysis of 62 RCTs found astragalus injection plus standard care improved ejection fraction and BNP in heart failure; a 2016 Cochrane review found formulas may aid chemotherapy as complementary support.
how: Add 9-15 g dried root slices to soups or simmer 30+ minutes, then discard the fibrous root. Capsules 500-1000 mg standardized extract 2-3 times daily; tincture 2-4 mL three times daily. Classic food therapy simmers it with chicken, goji and jujube.
safety: Very well tolerated. Avoid during acute febrile infection. May interact with immunosuppressive drugs (transplant and autoimmune medications) by stimulating immunity, and theoretically with lithium. Use only verified A. membranaceus, as other species contain toxic swainsonine.
origin: A premier Qi tonic that strengthens Wei Qi, the defensive energy, and heals chronic sores.

name: Reishi Mushroom
summary: A 2016 Cochrane review found reishi stimulated host immunity and patients were 1.27x more likely to respond to chemo or radiotherapy as complementary support alongside standard care, never replacing it. A 2012 study found 1.8 g extract reduced fatigue in neurasthenia.
how: Extract capsules 1.5-9 g dried extract daily, or 1-1.5 g concentrated extract specifying beta-glucan and triterpene content. Decoction: 5-10 g sliced reishi simmered 2+ hours (very bitter). Dual-extraction tinctures capture both compound classes.
safety: May increase bleeding risk and interact with anticoagulants and immunosuppressants; stop 2 weeks before surgery. Can lower blood pressure, so use caution on antihypertensives. Causes dry mouth, dizziness, nosebleeds and digestive upset; rare hepatotoxicity with powdered products.
origin: The 'Mushroom of Immortality', reserved for emperors; nourishes the Heart and calms the Shen.

name: Lion's Mane Mushroom
summary: Hericenones and erinacines stimulate nerve growth factor synthesis. A 2009 double-blind RCT found 3 g/day for 16 weeks improved cognitive scores in mild cognitive impairment (fading after stopping), and a 2010 RCT reduced depression and anxiety scores.
how: Standardized extract 500-1000 mg two to three times daily, ideally standardized to hericenones and erinacines. Powder 3-5 g daily in coffee, smoothies or soup; fresh mushroom sears like a steak. Cognitive benefits need weeks to months of consistent use.
safety: Generally very safe with few side effects. Possible allergy in those sensitive to mushrooms, plus mild initial digestive discomfort. May slow blood clotting, so use caution before surgery and with anticoagulants. Theoretical concern about stimulating NGF in certain cancers, unobserved in practice.
origin: Used in TCM to strengthen the Spleen, nourish the Stomach and calm the mind; the 'monkey head mushroom'.

name: Cordyceps
aka: Dong Chong Xia Cao, Cordyceps militaris/sinensis
summary: A 2017 RCT found Cordyceps militaris improved VO2max by 7% after 3 weeks, with cordycepin raising ATP production. A systematic review of 22 Chinese RCTs found it improved serum creatinine as an adjunct in chronic kidney disease.
how: Cultivated C. militaris extract 1-3 g daily, the sustainable option with equal or greater cordycepin than wild. CS-4 fermented mycelium 1.5-3 g daily is the form used in most studies. Powder blends into smoothies or broth, or simmer with chicken.
safety: Generally well tolerated, with mild GI upset, dry mouth or nausea. Theoretical interaction with immunosuppressive drugs and caution with anticoagulants, since it may slow clotting. May lower blood sugar, so monitor if diabetic. Avoid if allergic to molds; caution with hormone-sensitive conditions.
origin: 'Winter worm, summer grass', a prized tonic for both Kidney Yang and Lung Yin.

name: Turmeric / Curcumin
summary: Curcumin inhibits NF-kB, COX-2 and inflammatory cytokines. A 2016 meta-analysis of 8 RCTs found reduced osteoarthritis pain comparable to ibuprofen, a 2017 meta-analysis found antidepressant-scale benefit, and trials support it as complementary support in several cancers.
how: Standardized extract 500-1000 mg daily with black pepper and fat, since absorption alone is under 1%; phytosome forms such as Meriva absorb far better. Golden milk: 1 tsp turmeric plus a pinch of pepper in warm milk with honey.
safety: High doses cause GI upset, nausea and diarrhea. Curcumin inhibits platelet aggregation (caution with anticoagulants) and may lower blood sugar. Avoid concentrated supplements with gallstones or bile duct obstruction. High doses raise oxalate (kidney stones) and may interact with certain chemotherapy drugs, so consult your oncologist.
origin: In TCM Jiang Huang invigorates Blood and moves Qi, used for Blood-stasis pain in the shoulders and arms.

name: Green Tea
aka: Lu Cha, Camellia sinensis, matcha, EGCG
summary: A 2020 study of over 100,000 Chinese adults found habitual tea drinkers had 20% lower heart disease and stroke risk and lived 1.26 years longer. A 17-RCT meta-analysis found reduced fasting glucose and HbA1c.
how: Brew at 160-180 F (not boiling) for 2-3 minutes, re-steeping 2-3 times; 3-5 cups daily is the intake linked to benefit. Matcha delivers the whole leaf. EGCG supplements 300-500 mg daily, though whole tea is preferred.
safety: Contains 30-50 mg caffeine per cup, causing insomnia, anxiety or jitteriness. EGCG supplements above 800 mg/day are linked to liver toxicity, so keep doses moderate. Tannins reduce iron absorption. May interact with beta-blockers such as nadolol, blood thinners and stimulants, and can reduce absorption of some medications.
origin: In TCM green tea clears heat, resolves toxins and calms the mind; its discovery is credited to emperor Shennong.

name: Goji Berries
aka: Gou Qi Zi, wolfberry, Lycium barbarum
summary: Among the richest sources of zeaxanthin: a 2011 RCT found 15 g/day for 90 days raised plasma zeaxanthin 26% and protected against macular hypopigmentation, an early sign of macular degeneration. A 2009 RCT showed better influenza vaccine response in elders.
how: Eat 15-30 g dried berries daily as a snack or in oatmeal and salads. Tea: steep a handful 10 minutes and eat the berries afterward. Add to chicken soup with astragalus and jujube dates, or blend into smoothies.
safety: May interact with warfarin via CYP2C9, with several case reports of raised INR. Can lower blood sugar, so monitor on diabetes medications, and may add to blood pressure medications. Possible allergy in people reacting to nightshades such as tomatoes and peppers.
origin: A premier Yin tonic that nourishes Liver and Kidney and 'brightens the eyes'.

name: Schisandra
aka: Wu Wei Zi, five-flavor berry, Schisandra chinensis
summary: An adaptogen studied extensively by Soviet researchers; schisandrin B modulates cortisol and the HPA axis and is potently hepatoprotective, with the derivative DDB approved as a liver drug in several Asian countries. A 2017 review found improved attention under stress.
how: Chew 1-3 g dried berries daily, or steep 5-10 berries 10 minutes as tea. Tincture 1-2 mL two to three times daily; standardized extract 500-1000 mg daily. Traditionally brewed with goji and chrysanthemum.
safety: Can stimulate uterine contractions, so avoid in pregnancy. May interact with drugs metabolized by CYP3A4 and CYP1A2 and with CNS-active medications, and may lower seizure threshold, so use caution with epilepsy drugs. May cause heartburn and reduced appetite; avoid during acute febrile infection.
origin: Named for containing all five tastes, so it enters all five Yin organs, astringing Lung Qi and calming the Heart.

name: Licorice Root
summary: Deglycyrrhizinated licorice heals gastric and duodenal ulcers by boosting mucus and mucosal blood flow; a 1978 BMJ study found DGL as effective as cimetidine. Glycyrrhizin is antiviral and is used intravenously for hepatitis in Japan.
how: DGL chewable tablets 380-760 mg about 20 minutes before meals; this form removes glycyrrhizin and its blood pressure effect. Licorice root tea: 1-5 g simmered 10-15 minutes, 1-2 cups daily. Do not take whole licorice beyond 4-6 weeks.
safety: Major warning: glycyrrhizin causes sodium retention and potassium loss leading to hypertension, edema and hypokalemia, with hospitalizations and deaths from excess. Contraindicated in hypertension, heart failure, kidney disease and hypokalemia, and it strongly interacts with diuretics, corticosteroids, digoxin and blood pressure drugs. Avoid in pregnancy; cap whole root near 3 g daily.
origin: 'The Great Harmonizer', in an estimated 50-70% of classical TCM formulas to moderate other herbs.

name: Dong Quai
aka: Dang Gui, female ginseng, Angelica sinensis
summary: The premier Blood tonic in TCM. Ferulic acid promotes red blood cell production, and ligustilide adds antiplatelet, antithrombotic and vasodilatory effects used in Chinese hospitals for stroke and angina. Trials of it alone failed for menopause, since TCM never uses it singly.
how: Best used within a practitioner-prescribed formula, classically Si Wu Tang. Decoction 6-12 g dried root simmered 20-30 minutes; capsules or extract 500-1000 mg two to three times daily. Traditionally simmered with chicken and goji berries.
safety: Contains coumarins and interacts strongly with warfarin and other blood thinners. Furanocoumarins cause photosensitivity, so limit sun exposure. Avoid in pregnancy (uterine stimulation) and during heavy menstrual bleeding, since it invigorates Blood. Mild estrogenic activity means caution in estrogen-sensitive conditions.
origin: Called 'The Female Ginseng' but used for anyone with Blood deficiency, including men.

name: Chrysanthemum
summary: Contains lutein, beta-carotene and flavonoids that protect retinal cells, with a 2015 study showing protection against UV-induced retinal damage. Chlorogenic acid gives strong free-radical scavenging, and flavonoids lower blood pressure in animal studies.
how: Tea: steep 5-8 dried flowers 5-10 minutes, optionally with goji berries and rock sugar, one of China's most popular daily teas. Eye compress: brew strong tea, soak cotton pads and rest on closed eyes 10-15 minutes.
safety: Allergic reactions occur in people allergic to ragweed, daisies or the Asteraceae family, and it may interact with medications metabolized by the liver. Very safe at tea doses, though its cooling nature does not suit cold digestive constitutions with frequent diarrhea.
origin: Ju Hua disperses Wind, clears Heat and 'brightens the eyes', which in TCM are the window of the Liver.

name: Cinnamon / Cassia
aka: Rou Gui, Gui Zhi, Cinnamomum cassia
summary: A 2019 meta-analysis of 18 RCTs found cinnamon significantly reduced fasting glucose, cholesterol, LDL and triglycerides while raising HDL in type 2 diabetes, at 120 mg to 6 g/day. MHCP mimics insulin, with a 2003 study showing 18-29% glucose reductions.
how: Powder 1-6 g (1/4 to 1 tsp) daily in food, oatmeal or tea; a stick simmered 15 minutes makes tea. Capsules 500-1000 mg cassia two to three times daily with meals for blood sugar.
safety: Cassia holds up to 1% coumarin, liver-toxic in quantity; EFSA's tolerable intake is about 1-2 tsp of cassia for a 70 kg adult, and low-coumarin Ceylon cinnamon suits long-term use. May interact with diabetes medications (hypoglycemia) and blood thinners, and high doses lower blood pressure. Never apply cinnamon oil neat, as it burns skin.
origin: Rou Gui (bark) warms Kidney Yang; Gui Zhi (twigs) anchors the classic formula Gui Zhi Tang.

name: Jujube Dates
aka: Da Zao, Suan Zao Ren, Ziziphus jujuba
summary: Jujube seed (Suan Zao Ren) contains jujubosides with sedative and anxiolytic action through GABAergic and serotonergic pathways; a 2020 systematic review of 13 studies found jujube seed preparations improved sleep quality. The fruit is very high in vitamin C.
how: Eat 3-6 dried dates daily or add to teas, soups and congee. Jujube tea: simmer 5-6 sliced dates with ginger and goji berries 20 minutes. For sleep, Suan Zao Ren 15-30 g simmered, or 300-600 mg extract 30 minutes before bed.
safety: Very safe in food amounts. High sugar content means diabetics should account for it, and excess may cause bloating. Suan Zao Ren may add to sedative medications. In TCM it may slow digestion in those with dampness or phlegm.
origin: Da Zao tonifies Spleen Qi, nourishes Blood and calms the spirit; with licorice, a top harmonizing herb.

name: Kudzu
summary: Harvard/McLean research found puerarin cut binge drinking by 50% in a controlled lab setting, with a 2013 RCT confirming reduced beer consumption when taken before drinking. Puerarin is used intravenously in Chinese hospitals for angina and myocardial infarction.
how: For alcohol reduction, 1.5-3 g extract standardized to puerarin 30-60 minutes before anticipated drinking. Root decoction: 9-15 g simmered 20-30 minutes; the starchy root is also eaten. Capsules 500-1000 mg two to three times daily.
safety: May interact with diabetes medications (hypoglycemia), with anticoagulants via antiplatelet effects, and with methotrexate through shared liver enzymes. It is phytoestrogenic, so use caution in estrogen-sensitive conditions such as breast cancer, endometriosis and fibroids.
origin: Ge Gen releases the neck and upper back muscles and leads the classical formula Ge Gen Tang.

name: Fo-Ti
aka: He Shou Wu, Zhi He Shou Wu, Polygonum multiflorum
summary: A famous longevity tonic containing TSG, a resveratrol-related stilbene that extends lifespan and protects neurons in animals and promotes melanocyte proliferation in vitro, a mechanism for its anti-graying reputation. A Chinese trial found processed fo-ti cut total cholesterol 20%.
how: Use only the processed form (Zhi He Shou Wu, steamed with black soybean juice); raw fo-ti is a harsh laxative and more hepatotoxic. Decoction 9-15 g simmered 30+ minutes, or extract 500-1000 mg two to three times daily.
safety: Liver toxicity warning: raw and processed fo-ti have both been linked to hepatotoxicity including liver failure, with warnings issued in the UK, Australia and Europe. Liver function monitoring is strongly recommended; avoid in liver disease and alongside hepatotoxic medications. Avoid in pregnancy and breastfeeding; may cause diarrhea and nausea.
origin: A classic Jing (essence) tonic said to restore hair color and strengthen tendons and bones.

name: Sweet Wormwood / Artemisinin
summary: Tu Youyou isolated artemisinin from this herb guided by TCM texts, earning the 2015 Nobel Prize; artemisinin combination therapies are the WHO first-line malaria treatment. Derivatives show anticancer activity in preclinical models only, an early-stage complementary support area.
how: For malaria, artemisinin-based combination therapy is prescription-only under medical supervision, never self-treatment. Traditional tea steeps leaves in warm (not boiling) water, which preserves artemisinin, as a supplement only. Artemisinin capsules of 100-200 mg exist but quality varies.
safety: Do not self-treat malaria, and the WHO advises against Artemisia annua tea as monotherapy because it promotes drug resistance. Causes nausea, vomiting, dizziness and tinnitus, and is neurotoxic at high doses (brainstem and auditory damage in animals). Embryotoxic, so absolutely avoid in pregnancy; may interact with CYP2B6 and CYP3A4 substrates.
origin: Ge Hong's 340 CE text described wringing juice from soaked Qing Hao, a cold extraction preserving the active compound.

name: Dan Shen
summary: Tanshinones and salvianolic acids improve circulation and are used intravenously in Chinese hospitals for acute coronary syndrome. A 2007 Cochrane review found benefit for angina when combined with conventional treatment.
how: Decoction 9-15 g; Danshen dripping pills are widely used in China. Best taken under practitioner guidance alongside conventional cardiac care.
safety: Strong anticoagulant interaction with warfarin: do not combine. Because it addresses serious cardiac conditions, use only alongside proper medical management, never as a substitute.
origin: A classic Blood-moving herb for blood stasis and chest pain.

name: Bai Zhu
summary: Used for digestive weakness, diarrhea, edema and fatigue. Atractylone stimulates gastric motility, and the herb has been studied within formulas for IBS and chemotherapy-induced nausea.
how: Typically 6-15 g within a multi-herb decoction prescribed by a TCM practitioner rather than taken alone.
safety: No major interactions are documented, but it is traditionally used in formula: consult a qualified practitioner and tell your doctor if you take prescription medications.
origin: A core Spleen Qi tonic that dries dampness in classical Chinese formulas.

name: Huang Qin
summary: Baicalin and baicalein are potent anti-inflammatories and antivirals with strong antioxidant activity, studied in Chinese trials as adjunct COVID-19 therapy and used for inflammation, infection, anxiety and allergies.
how: Typically 6-15 g in decoction, usually within a formula prescribed by a TCM practitioner.
safety: Rare hepatotoxicity has been reported, so avoid in liver disease, watch for jaundice or dark urine, and use reputable products. Consult a practitioner before combining with prescription medications.
origin: A classic heat-clearing, damp-drying herb in Chinese formulas.

name: Ashwagandha
aka: Withania somnifera, Indian ginseng, winter cherry
summary: Strongest evidence is for stress: a 2012 RCT found 300 mg root extract twice daily cut cortisol 27.9% and anxiety scores 44%. Trials also show higher testosterone and sperm count in infertile men, greater muscle mass, and a 2020 meta-analysis found improved sleep.
how: KSM-66 root extract 300-600 mg daily, the most studied form, or Sensoril 125-250 mg daily. Traditionally 1 tsp powder in warm milk with honey before bed, or root powder 3-6 g daily. Benefits accumulate over 4-8 weeks.
safety: Can raise thyroid hormone: avoid in hyperthyroidism, caution with thyroid medication. May enhance sedatives, anxiolytics and immunosuppressants and interact with blood pressure and blood sugar medications. Avoid in pregnancy (abortifacient at high doses). Rare liver injury reported; women with PCOS should be cautious.
origin: A premier Rasayana whose name means 'smell of the horse', for the vitality it confers.

name: Tulsi / Holy Basil
aka: Ocimum tenuiflorum, O. sanctum, Queen of Herbs
summary: A 2017 review of 24 studies found significant adaptogenic and anti-stress effects with cortisol modulation. A 2017 review of 9 clinical trials found reduced fasting and postprandial glucose and HbA1c, and a 2014 trial found 300 mg/day improved FEV1 and PEFR in asthma.
how: Tulsi tea: steep 5-8 fresh leaves or 1 tsp dried 5-10 minutes, 2-3 cups daily, the traditional form. Capsules 300-600 mg standardized extract two to three times daily; tincture 30-40 drops two to three times daily.
safety: May reduce fertility (animal antifertility and anti-spermatogenic effects), so couples trying to conceive should be cautious. Eugenol slows clotting: stop 2 weeks before surgery and use caution with anticoagulant and antiplatelet drugs. May lower blood sugar with diabetes medications and enhance pentobarbital and other CNS depressants.
origin: The most sacred plant in Hinduism, a Rasayana balancing all three doshas and grown in most households.

name: Triphala
summary: A 2017 RCT found triphala improved bowel movements, consistency and straining in functional constipation better than senna with fewer side effects. A 2019 study showed more Bifidobacterium, Lactobacillus and butyrate, and triphala mouthwash matched chlorhexidine for plaque.
how: Powder 3-6 g (1/2 to 1 tsp) in warm water before bed, the traditional method, with honey for the sour taste. Tablets 500-1000 mg two to three times daily before meals or at bedtime; steep 1 tsp powder for a cooled mouthwash.
safety: May cause loose stools, cramping or gas at first, so start low. Avoid in pregnancy, since haritaki mildly stimulates the uterus. Use caution with diabetes medications (may lower blood sugar) and it may increase anticoagulant effects via amalaki's vitamin C. Not for acute diarrhea, which needs evaluation.
origin: Ayurveda's most prescribed formula, a Tridoshic Rasayana praised in the Charaka Samhita.

name: Brahmi
summary: A 2014 meta-analysis of 9 RCTs (518 subjects) found significantly improved attention, cognitive processing and working memory, with stronger effects past 12 weeks. Bacosides modulate serotonin, dopamine and acetylcholine and reduce beta-amyloid aggregation; trials also show reduced anxiety.
how: Standardized extract 300-450 mg daily at 50% bacosides, with a fat-containing meal since bacosides are fat-soluble. Traditional Brahmi ghrita cooks the powder in ghee, 1 tsp daily; powder 5-10 g in warm milk. Allow 8-12 weeks.
safety: Commonly causes GI upset, nausea and cramping, so take with food. May raise thyroid hormone (caution in hyperthyroidism), cause drowsiness and enhance CNS depressants. Possible interaction with cholinergic drugs such as donepezil and with anticholinergics. It raises gastric acid, so use caution with ulcers; avoid in pregnancy and breastfeeding.
origin: A leading Medhya Rasayana named after Brahma, given to students to sharpen memory and learning.

name: Neem
summary: Azadirachtin, nimbin and nimbidin act against bacteria including MRSA, fungi, viruses and parasites. A 2011 RCT found neem mouthwash reduced plaque and gingivitis as effectively as chlorhexidine, and reviews find leaf extract lowers blood glucose in animal and small human trials.
how: Leaf capsules 300-600 mg two to three times daily internally; leaf tea from 5-10 dried leaves steeped 10 minutes (extremely bitter). Apply diluted neem oil externally for fungal infections, eczema, acne or as insect repellent; chew a fresh twig (datun) for oral care.
safety: Never ingest neem oil, which is toxic internally and has poisoned children; only leaves and bark are used internally, and not orally for young children. Lowers blood sugar sharply with diabetes drugs. Reduces fertility in both sexes and may cause miscarriage, so avoid when conceiving, pregnant or nursing. Immunostimulatory, so avoid with immunosuppressants and autoimmune disease; high or prolonged doses harm liver and kidneys.
origin: Called 'Sarva Roga Nivarini' (curer of all ailments); every part of the tree is used.

name: Moringa
summary: A 2019 systematic review of 10 clinical trials found leaf powder at 1-8 g/day significantly reduced fasting glucose in type 2 diabetes, and a 2000 study found 8 g daily for 40 days lowered cholesterol, LDL and triglycerides. Moringin is a potent NF-kB inhibitor, and reviews support galactagogue use.
how: Leaf powder 1-2 tsp (3-6 g) daily in smoothies or soups, starting at 1/2 tsp. Capsules 400-800 mg two to three times daily. Cook fresh leaves like spinach, steep dried leaves as tea, or use drumstick pods in curries.
safety: Avoid moringa root, root bark and seed extracts, which contain toxic, paralytic spirochin. May lower blood sugar and blood pressure, so monitor with relevant medications, and may interact with thyroid medications (goitrogens) and CYP3A4-metabolized drugs. High doses showed antifertility effects in animals; start small to avoid digestive upset.
origin: In Ayurveda Shigru reduces swelling, destroys worms and kindles digestive fire.

name: Amla
summary: One of the richest natural vitamin C sources, uniquely stabilized by tannins. A 2012 RCT found 500 mg extract twice daily comparable to atorvastatin 20 mg for lowering cholesterol, LDL and triglycerides while raising HDL, and studies show reduced fasting glucose and HbA1c.
how: Powder 3-6 g daily in warm water with honey, the traditional dose, or fresh juice 20-30 mL on an empty stomach. Chyawanprash 1-2 tsp daily; capsules 500-1000 mg two to three times daily. Warm amla oil massaged into the scalp for hair.
safety: Very high vitamin C may cause GI upset or diarrhea at high doses, and its acidity can aggravate reflux. May lower blood sugar with diabetes medications and enhance anticoagulants through antiplatelet activity. High vitamin C increases iron absorption, so use caution in hemochromatosis.
origin: Charaka Samhita calls it the best rejuvenative; it bases Chyawanprash and is one of the three Triphala fruits.

name: Shatavari
summary: A 2018 systematic review found shatavari raised prolactin and milk production in animal and small human studies, and a 2018 RCT found 250 mg root extract twice daily reduced hot flashes and night sweats. Animal work shows gastroprotection comparable to ranitidine.
how: Powder 3-6 g daily in warm milk with ghee and honey, the traditional absorption-boosting preparation. Capsules 500-1000 mg two to three times daily; tincture 2-4 mL two to three times daily. Shatavari ghrita is the classical reproductive preparation.
safety: Avoid if allergic to asparagus. It may be estrogenic, so avoid in estrogen-receptor-positive breast cancer and other estrogen-sensitive conditions, and it may interact with diuretics. Avoid in acute kidney inflammation, acute diarrhea or heavy mucus conditions; may cause weight gain.
origin: Ayurveda's premier female reproductive tonic, the counterpart to ashwagandha, nourishing reproductive tissue and Ojas.

name: Guggul
summary: Guggulsterones antagonize the farnesoid X receptor governing cholesterol metabolism; Indian trials showed 10-27% reductions in cholesterol and triglycerides, but a 2003 JAMA RCT found guggul raised LDL in a Western population. A 2003 pilot study matched tetracycline for nodulocystic acne.
how: Standardized extract 500-1000 mg three times daily at 2.5-5% guggulsterones. Classical formulas include Kaishore Guggulu for joints and gout, Triphala Guggulu for detoxification and Yogaraj Guggulu for Vata pain, as a practitioner directs.
safety: The JAMA LDL finding means lipid monitoring is advised. It stimulates thyroid function, so avoid in hyperthyroidism, and it interacts with thyroid medications, blood thinners, cardiovascular drugs and oral contraceptives, reducing propranolol and diltiazem efficacy. Avoid in pregnancy and breastfeeding; may cause nausea, loose stools and rash.
origin: A key Lekhana (scraping) resin; the Sushruta Samhita described it for atherosclerosis 2,500 years ago.

name: Arjuna
summary: A landmark 2001 RCT found bark powder 500 mg every 8 hours improved ejection fraction, exercise tolerance and NYHA class in chronic stable heart failure, and a 2002 crossover study matched isosorbide mononitrate for angina. Arjunolic acid inhibits ACE.
how: Traditional Arjuna Kshira Paka: boil 3-6 g bark powder in one cup milk and one cup water until reduced to one cup, taken on an empty stomach each morning. Bark powder 3-6 g daily; capsules 500 mg two to three times daily; Arjunarishta 15-30 mL after meals.
safety: Never use as a substitute for emergency cardiac care; use under medical supervision. May lower blood pressure, so monitor with antihypertensives, and it may interact with cardiac glycosides such as digoxin, anticoagulants and blood pressure medications. Can cause constipation and headache; pregnancy safety is not established.
origin: The primary Ayurvedic heart tonic (Hrdya), named after the Mahabharata warrior.

name: Turmeric (Ayurvedic use)
summary: Haridra is used for inflammation, skin disease, diabetes and anemia. The traditional Golden Paste of turmeric with black pepper and ghee or coconut oil was validated millennia later by research showing piperine and fat dramatically raise curcumin absorption.
how: Golden Paste combines turmeric powder, black pepper and coconut oil or ghee. Haldi doodh: turmeric in warm milk with pepper, ghee and honey before bed. Turmeric paste goes on cuts, burns and skin conditions; Nasya drops turmeric in warm ghee into the nostrils.
safety: Same cautions as concentrated curcumin: it inhibits platelet aggregation (caution with anticoagulants) and may lower blood sugar. Avoid concentrated supplements with gallstones or bile duct obstruction. High doses raise oxalate (kidney stone risk) and may interact with certain chemotherapy drugs, so consult your oncologist. Food amounts are safe.
origin: Bitter, pungent and heating, balancing all three doshas and used for Kushtha (skin disease) and Prameha.

name: Cardamom
summary: A 2009 RCT found 3 g cardamom powder daily for 12 weeks significantly reduced systolic and diastolic blood pressure, raised antioxidant status 90% and increased fibrinolytic activity in stage 1 hypertension. 1,8-cineole is anti-inflammatory and it is a validated carminative.
how: Chew a pod after meals for digestion and fresh breath. In chai, crush 2-3 pods with ginger and cinnamon. Powder 1/4-1/2 tsp in coffee or baking; for blood pressure, 3 g (about 1 tsp) daily per the clinical study.
safety: Very safe at culinary doses. May interact with anticoagulant medications. Gallstone patients should use caution, since it stimulates bile flow. High doses cause GI discomfort, and allergic reactions are rare but possible.
origin: 'The Queen of Spices', Tridoshic in Ayurveda and used to kindle digestive fire and treat vomiting and asthma.

name: Black Pepper / Piperine
summary: Piperine inhibits CYP3A4, CYP2D6, CYP1A2 and P-glycoprotein, raising curcumin absorption by 2,000% plus meaningful boosts to CoQ10, B6, beta-carotene and selenium. It is also thermogenic, anti-inflammatory via NF-kB, and raises brain serotonin and dopamine in animals.
how: Use freshly ground pepper liberally in cooking, where piperine is highest. Trikatu: equal parts black pepper, long pepper and dried ginger, 1/4-1/2 tsp with honey before meals. BioPerine 5-20 mg with other supplements; always pair with turmeric.
safety: Critical interaction: piperine raises absorption of medications too, dramatically increasing levels of phenytoin, propranolol, theophylline, rifampin, some chemotherapy drugs, cyclosporine and statins, so tell your doctor if you supplement it. It raises gastric acid, so avoid high supplemental doses with ulcers or GERD. Cooking amounts are safe.
origin: 'The King of Spices', a Trikatu ingredient that kindles Agni and destroys Ama.

name: Ghee
summary: Contains 3-4% butyric acid, the short-chain fatty acid fueling colonocytes, reducing intestinal inflammation and supporting gut barrier integrity, plus CLA (up to 5x more grass-fed). It enhances absorption of fat-soluble vitamins and curcumin, validating cooking herbs in ghee.
how: Use 1-2 tsp as a cooking fat; its 485 F smoke point suits high heat. Mix herbal powders such as turmeric or brahmi into warm ghee to boost absorption. A traditional ritual takes 1 tsp warm ghee on an empty stomach. Keep to 1-3 tsp daily.
safety: High in calories and saturated fat, so portion control matters and those with high cholesterol, heart disease or obesity should use it sparingly and monitor lipids. Trace dairy proteins remain, so highly dairy-allergic people should test cautiously. Ayurveda deems equal ghee and honey incompatible; Kapha types should limit it.
origin: Charaka called ghee the best of all oils; it is the primary Anupana (carrier) for Ayurvedic medicines.

name: Coconut Oil
aka: Narikela Taila, Cocos nucifera, virgin coconut oil
summary: About 50% lauric acid, converted to antimicrobial monolaurin active against S. aureus, Candida, H. pylori and enveloped viruses. A 2016 systematic review found oil pulling reduced S. mutans, plaque and gingival inflammation comparably to chlorhexidine.
how: Oil pulling: swish 1 tbsp virgin oil 15-20 minutes each morning before brushing, then spit into the trash. Cook with 1-2 tsp at medium heat. Apply to skin or hair as a moisturizer or mask; blend 1 tsp into coffee for MCT energy.
safety: Roughly 82% saturated fat, the highest of any common dietary fat. A 2020 Circulation meta-analysis found it significantly raises LDL versus non-tropical plant oils, and the AHA advises against it as a primary cooking fat for cardiovascular patients. Comedogenic on the face for some; calorie-dense at 120 cal/tbsp.
origin: Narikela pacifies Vata and Pitta and is the base oil for Abhyanga massage in Kerala's healing tradition.

name: Guduchi / Giloy
summary: A potent immunomodulator used for immune deficiency, fever, diabetes, gout and allergies. It contains berberine and tinosporin with anti-inflammatory and antiviral effects, and a 2020 study during COVID-19 found giloy extract improved immune markers.
how: Extract 500-1000 mg daily, or 15-30 mL fresh juice daily.
safety: Indian case reports from 2021-2022 raised liver injury concerns, with contamination by other plants suspected, so buy only from verified sources and avoid with existing liver disease. As an immunostimulant, use caution with immunosuppressants and autoimmune conditions.
origin: Called 'Amrita', the nectar of immortality, in Ayurveda.

name: Pippali / Long Pepper
summary: Used for respiratory conditions, digestion and enhancing the bioavailability of other remedies. It contains piperine like black pepper plus piperlongumine, which has anticancer properties studied in preclinical models only.
how: Powder 1-3 g daily, classically as one third of the Trikatu formula with black pepper and dried ginger.
safety: Same critical drug interaction as black pepper and piperine: it raises blood levels of many medications including phenytoin, propranolol, theophylline, rifampin, cyclosporine, statins and some chemotherapy drugs. Inform your doctor before supplementing.
origin: One of the 'three pungents' in Trikatu, Ayurveda's classic digestive formula.

name: Shankhpushpi
summary: Another Medhya Rasayana used for anxiety, insomnia, cognitive decline and epilepsy. Animal studies show anxiolytic, memory-enhancing and anticonvulsant effects via GABAergic and cholinergic mechanisms, with limited but promising human data.
how: Powder 3-6 g daily, or 500 mg standardized extract daily.
safety: May interact with anti-epileptic and thyroid medications, so consult your prescriber before use. Given its sedative profile, use caution with other CNS depressants.
origin: A classical Ayurvedic brain rejuvenator for calming the mind.

name: Manjistha
summary: Used for skin conditions, blood purification and lymphatic congestion. Alizarin and purpurin have anti-inflammatory, antioxidant and hepatoprotective effects, and it is used clinically for acne, eczema and pigmentation disorders, though trial data are limited.
how: Powder 3-6 g daily, or 500-1000 mg extract daily.
safety: Use caution with anticoagulants. It harmlessly stains urine and sweat red or brown, which can be mistaken for bleeding.
origin: A classical Ayurvedic Raktashodhaka (blood-cleansing) herb for skin and lymph.
